question: Why do residual connections make very deep networks easier to train?

definition.title: Why residual connections help very deep networks train
definition.summary: Residual connections preserve an input path and let layers learn corrections, making optimization easier without guaranteeing that every deeper network trains well.

scenes.title: Learn a correction to the input

beats.caption: The stacked layers learn a residual: the correction F(x) = H(x) − x needed to reach the desired mapping H(x).
beats.explanation: The paper changes what the layers must learn. They learn a change relative to their input rather than the entire desired mapping.

beats.caption: The shortcut carries x unchanged, and addition combines it with the learned correction.
beats.explanation: This identity shortcut skips the stacked layers. The diagram shows the addition; the original block applies a nonlinearity afterward.

beats.caption: If preserving the input is useful, the residual layers can aim for zero.
beats.explanation: Then x + F(x) becomes x at the addition. The authors hypothesize that pushing a residual toward zero is easier than making stacked nonlinear layers learn an identity mapping.

scenes.title: Addition works one entry at a time

beats.caption: In this illustration, the shortcut preserves all three input entries.
beats.explanation: These invented values represent a small feature vector. A real residual block can operate on much larger feature tensors.

beats.caption: The residual branch supplies changes: increase one entry, decrease another, and leave the third alone.
beats.explanation: The illustrative correction is [1, −1, 0]. Residuals need not be small; these values simply make the operation visible.

beats.caption: Adding corresponding entries gives [3, 4, 1], preserving the third entry without rebuilding it.
beats.explanation: This illustrates the sum before activation. Element-wise addition requires matching shapes; the paper uses a shortcut projection when dimensions must change.

rows.label: Identity
cells: Zero residual preserves x at addition

rows.label: Gradient
cells: Through every layer in the stack

beats.caption: Extra layers become easier to optimize when preserving a useful representation is an accessible solution.
beats.explanation: The paper shows that a deeper plain network can have higher training error, so added capacity alone does not solve optimization. Residual learning eases this degradation problem.

beats.caption: The shortcut also gives gradients a direct route across the residual branch.
beats.explanation: As background calculus, the derivative of x + F(x) is I + J_F, where I is the identity and J_F is the residual's derivative. This route helps gradient propagation, but subsequent activations and repeated blocks mean it does not guarantee nonvanishing gradients.

takeaways: Residual layers learn how to change an input while a shortcut carries it forward.
A zero residual makes preserving the input easy at the addition.
Easier optimization and a direct gradient path help make much deeper networks trainable.
